interstellar-ships.who_owns: A ship built to travel to another star would stay under the legal control of the country that lists it on its official register of space objects. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, says in Article VIII that this control continues 'while in outer space' and gives no distance at which it ends. No one has ruled on what happens to law on a voyage lasting many generations.
interstellar-ships.hook: The obstacle comes before departure. Under Article VI of the treaty, a private launch needs permission and continuing oversight from a country that has joined the treaty. The published page on Breakthrough Starshot does not discuss launch approval, and no known project has reached that stage.
interstellar-ships.can_you_build: No. Crewed ships exist only as studies and paper designs. The one funded plan for an uncrewed probe, Breakthrough Starshot, was reported in September 2025 to be on hold indefinitely.

rules.says: The country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space or on a planet, moon or other natural body in space.
Private space activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a country that has joined the treaty, and countries answer internationally for that activity.
Countries are liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage their space objects cause.

facts: Alpha Centauri, a star system, is 4.34 to 4.37 light-years away.
The Starshot probe plan began with US$100 million in funding and had spent about $4.5 million by 2025, according to Philip Lubin.
Project Persephone, a design concept for a 'worldship' that people would live on for generations, describes a vessel 20 km long and 5 km across carrying 50 to 500 people.
DARPA, the US military's research agency, gave the 100 Year Starship project $1 million and NASA's Ames center gave $100,000. The grant made in 2012 was $500,000.
118 countries had joined the Outer Space Treaty as of October 2025.

the-sun.who_owns: Nobody owns it in law, though the wording leaves room for argument. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, bars 'national appropriation', meaning a country taking something as its own, and does not mention private people. María Ángeles Durán, a Spanish woman who claims the Sun, argues that this stops countries from owning a star and leaves individuals free to do so. One article, on the site Genbeta, says a Spanish court rejected private ownership of the Sun in 2016, but it names no court document.
the-sun.hook: No one can reach the Sun, so any limits come from people and offices on Earth: the notary who records a deed, the rules of the website used to sell plots, and a local court.
the-sun.can_you_build: Nothing can be built. The only activity on record is paperwork and online sales of plots at one euro per square metre.

rules.says: Bars 'national appropriation' of outer space, including natural bodies in space, meaning no country may take them as its own. Durán argues this does not reach a private person.

facts: Durán's deed to the Sun was recorded by a notary, an official who certifies legal documents, in 2010.
Plots were offered at 1 euro per square metre.
Her claim against eBay, the online auction site, is reported as 10,000 euros by The Register and about 7,500 pounds by Scottish Financial News.

outer-moons.who_owns: Nobody. Moons and dwarf planets are natural bodies in space, so they fall under the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, which bars any country from taking them as its own. The published descriptions of these settlement proposals do not discuss ownership or law at all.
outer-moons.hook: The country that registers a craft keeps legal power over it, and the responsible treaty country must give permission for private activity and keep overseeing it. The treaty text sets no distance limit on either rule. No craft has carried people this far, so none of this has been tested.
outer-moons.can_you_build: No crew has been sent under any of these plans. NASA's own study of a trip to Callisto, a moon of Jupiter, assumed major advances in propulsion for a round trip of about 2 to 5 years.

rules.says: Outer space, including the Moon and other natural bodies in space, cannot be taken over by any country, whether by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means.
Private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a country that has joined the treaty.

facts: Europa, a moon of Jupiter: unshielded radiation is about 5.40 sieverts (a measure of radiation dose) per day, and about 5 sieverts over a few days is fatal.
Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter: radiation is about 0.08 sieverts per day, and gravity is about 0.15 of Earth's.
Callisto, a moon of Jupiter: gravity is about 0.13 of Earth's, and it lies outside Jupiter's radiation belt.
Titan, a moon of Saturn: gravity is 0.138 of Earth's.
Enceladus, a moon of Saturn: its underground ocean lies only tens of metres under the ice at the south pole.

venus-clouds.who_owns: Nobody. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, says outer space, including planets, cannot be taken over by any country through a claim of authority, use, occupation or any other means. Nothing has been built there, so no one has tested whether a balloon drifting in the air of Venus counts as a space object or as use of the planet.
venus-clouds.hook: Private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from the responsible treaty country, and the country that registers the craft keeps legal power over it after it leaves Earth.
venus-clouds.can_you_build: No one has. Every proposal is a paper study. The one NASA study received no further funding and was canceled by 2017. The Soviet Union's Vega balloons floated in the atmosphere for only days, until their batteries ran out.

rules.says: Outer space, including the Moon and other natural bodies in space, cannot be taken over by any country, whether by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means.
Private activity in space needs permission and continuing oversight from a country that has joined the treaty, and countries answer for what their nationals do.

The country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space or on a planet, moon or other natural body in space.

facts: At 55 km above the surface: 27 C, air pressure of 0.5 bar (about half that at sea level on Earth), and gravity of 8.73 metres per second squared, according to NASA's HAVOC study.
At about 50 km: air pressure about the same as sea level on Earth and temperatures of 0 to 50 C, according to figures from Landis.
Breathable air would float in the carbon dioxide atmosphere of Venus, with over 60% of the lifting power helium has on Earth.
Winds at the cloud tops reach up to 95 metres per second, about 340 km per hour.

mars-and-beyond.who_owns: The same as the Moon: Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, bars any country from taking it over, and nothing in the treaty stops at the Moon's orbit. A private contract cannot change that. Starlink's test-phase customer terms in 2020 said the parties 'recognize Mars as a free planet', and that wording binds only the people who signed the contract.
mars-and-beyond.hook: Before departure, a mission needs a launching country, an entry on a register and a licence. Distance would make enforcement slow, but under Article VIII the registering country's legal power over the craft continues.
mars-and-beyond.can_you_build: No settlement has been attempted. A 2020 model by the researcher Salotti estimates about 110 people as the minimum for a self-sustaining Mars colony, under that model's assumptions.

rules.cite: Outer Space Treaty Art. II, VI, VIII, IX
rules.says: These articles bar any country from taking over a planet, require a country to oversee private activity, give legal power to the country that registers a craft, and impose a duty to avoid contaminating other worlds. All are written for natural bodies in space generally.
For the countries that have joined it, the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty that few countries have joined, extends to all bodies in the solar system other than Earth.
An international scientific standard on keeping other worlds free of contamination, last revised in January 2026. It works through national space agencies and has no treaty force of its own.

'No Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities' and disputes settle 'through self-governing principles'. This is a term in a private contract, as quoted by Universe Today. Whether the current text still says this has not been confirmed.

facts: Salotti 2020: a minimum of 110 settlers, published in the journal Scientific Reports.

asteroids.who_owns: The same as the Moon. No country can claim authority over an asteroid, because the treaties cover all natural bodies in space. Taking resources from one is still an open question, and US law allows its citizens to do it, subject to the international obligations of the US.
asteroids.hook: The same as the Moon. Under Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, a craft stays under the law of the country that registered it.
asteroids.can_you_build: No published plan to settle an asteroid has been found. Fraud has appeared here too: in 1999, officials at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the regulator of investment markets, listed share offerings for exploring a near-Earth asteroid among fraudulent internet schemes.

rules.says: No country may take over a planet, asteroid or other natural body in space.
For the countries that have joined it, the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty that few countries have joined, applies its Moon rules to other bodies in the solar system, except Earth.
Those rules do not apply to meteorites that reach Earth naturally.
US citizens may own resources they recover from asteroids, subject to the international obligations of the US.
The Artemis Accords, a set of principles that countries sign as a political commitment, say that extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body.

facts: A statement by the International Institute of Space Law (IISL), a professional body of space lawyers, says deed claims have been extended to other natural bodies in space. A deed seller told Discover magazine that he owns about 95 planetary bodies.

moon.who_owns: No country can own it, and the countries in the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, cannot take it over. Sellers of 'deeds' claim that private people can own land there, and the International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, has issued a statement warning that buyers may be misled. A second treaty with far fewer members, the Moon Agreement, adds a 'common heritage' rule for its 17 members, meaning the Moon belongs to humanity as a whole. In addition, 78 countries have signed the Artemis Accords, a set of principles that describe themselves as a political commitment.
moon.hook: Articles VI and VIII of the Outer Space Treaty bind the launching and registering country, so the practical limits are your own country's licensing and the register that lists your station. Article II bars any country from taking over the Moon by any means, and Article 11(3) of the Moon Agreement bars ownership of the surface for its members. A deed sold by a private person therefore appears to have no treaty supporting it.
moon.can_you_build: Any trip needs a launch licence and radio frequencies assigned through the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency that coordinates them. On the surface you have no right to keep others out, because Article I of the Outer Space Treaty gives free access to all areas, though the safety zones in the Accords may limit access in practice.

rules.says: No country may take over the Moon by claiming authority over it, by using or occupying it, or by any other means.
Natural bodies in space may be used for peaceful purposes only, with no military bases, weapons tests or military exercises.

rules.cite: Outer Space Treaty Art. VI, VIII
rules.says: Private activity needs permission. A registered object stays the property of its owner, and the country that registered it keeps legal power over it and its staff, on the surface as well.
Countries must avoid harmful contamination and pay due attention to the interests of others.

The Moon is the 'common heritage of mankind', meaning it belongs to humanity as a whole. Its surface and what lies below cannot become the property of any country, organization or person. A future set of rules is to govern commercial use of its resources.
Countries may build stations, using only the area they need, and must tell the UN.
Countries that sign say that extracting resources does not in itself count as a country taking over the body.
Countries that sign give notice of their operations and respect 'safety zones' around them.
US citizens may own and sell space resources they recover, subject to the international obligations of the US.

facts: 78 countries have signed the Artemis Accords, the latest being Vietnam on 28 October 2026, according to NASA.
The Moon Agreement had 17 member countries and 4 that had signed without joining as at 1 January 2026. Saudi Arabia withdrew with effect from 5 January 2024.
The Moon Agreement took effect in July 1984 after Austria became the fifth country to join.
The Moon's radius is about 1,740 km, and it is about 385,000 km from Earth, according to NASA.
The International Institute of Space Law's statement says claims of 'deeds to lunar property' raise the chance that individuals will be misled.

lagrange-cislunar.name: Lagrange points and the space between Earth and the Moon
lagrange-cislunar.who_owns: This is outer space, so the same rules apply as elsewhere in space, and no separate treaty covers it. Lagrange points are positions in space where objects tend to stay put, which saves spacecraft fuel. The definition of 'the moon' in the Moon Agreement, a treaty on the Moon and other bodies in the solar system, extends to orbits around it, but only 17 countries have joined that agreement.
lagrange-cislunar.hook: The same as low Earth orbit. A station here needs a launching country and an entry on a register, and it depends on Earth for radio frequencies and supplies.
lagrange-cislunar.can_you_build: The same launch, licence and radio frequency steps apply. No published plan for a private settlement here has been found.

rules.cite: Outer Space Treaty Art. I, II, VI, VIII
rules.says: The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, makes space free to use, bars any country from taking it over, makes countries responsible for space activity, and gives legal power over a craft to the country that registered it.
References to the Moon include orbits and paths around it.

Under the Artemis Accords, a set of principles for space activity, countries that sign commit to registering objects, releasing scientific data, and giving notice of operations inside 'safety zones' to avoid harmful interference. The Accords describe themselves as a political commitment.

facts: The Moon is about 385,000 km from Earth, according to NASA.
NASA describes five Lagrange points for a pair of large bodies such as the Earth and Sun. The NASA page reviewed gives no distances, so none is stated here.

geo.name: Geostationary orbit (where a satellite seems to hold one spot above Earth)
geo.who_owns: The same rules apply as in low Earth orbit under space law. In practice, positions in this orbit and radio frequencies are coordinated through the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio and satellite coordination, and its members are countries. Eight countries on the equator tried to claim the positions above them in 1976. Article II of the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, bars any country from taking over outer space. It does not name this orbit, so treating that declaration as conflicting with the treaty is an interpretation.
geo.hook: Radio frequencies. A frequency filing can only come from the national authority of a member country. A station without one would have no recorded protection from interference, and other operators would appear to have no duty to coordinate with it.
geo.can_you_build: To reach this orbit, a craft first follows a long oval path that climbs to 35,786 km, and then fires its engine again to round the path into a circle. Operating there means a filing by a country and a launch licence.

rules.says: No country may take over outer space. That this covers the geostationary orbit is an interpretation, since the treaty does not define outer space.
Member countries must treat radio frequencies and orbits, including the geostationary orbit, as limited natural resources and allow fair access to them.
Frequency assignments are entered in the Master International Frequency Register, the official global list, after national authorities submit notices.
Eight countries on the equator asserted full legal authority over the part of the orbit above them, according to Wikipedia.

facts: The orbit is 35,786 km above Earth, according to the European Space Agency.
The ITU has 194 member countries, according to the ITU.
Filings made since 7 November 1998 carry fees to recover the ITU's costs, under Resolution 88 and Council Decision 482.

orbital-megastructures.who_owns: A structure in orbit falls under the legal power of the country that lists it on its register of space objects. A space elevator, a proposed cable running from the ground up into orbit, would also touch Earth. Its anchor would sit on a country's land or at sea, and Wikipedia's page on the idea notes that ocean anchors are often placed in international waters, which could simplify talks over territory.
orbital-megastructures.hook: Launch licensing and liability rules on Earth, plus, for an elevator, the laws of whichever country or sea hosts the anchor.
orbital-megastructures.can_you_build: None has been built. The stated technical obstacle for elevators is the cable: Google X, Google's research lab, froze its project in 2014 after finding that no one had made a flawless carbon nanotube strand longer than a metre. Voyager Station is covered in its own separate entry.

rules.says: Under the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, the country that lists a space object on its register keeps legal power and control over the object and the people on it while it is in outer space or on a planet, moon or other natural body in space.
Countries are liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage caused by their space objects.
Private activity needs permission and continuing oversight from a country that has joined the treaty.

facts: Stanford torus (a ring-shaped space habitat design): a ring 1.8 km across, 10,000 residents, about 10 million metric tons.
Kalpana One (design revised in 2007): 250 m radius, 325 m long, 3,000 people.
Bishop Ring (1997 design): 1,000 km radius, about 3 million km2 of land.
McKendree cylinder (1995 design): 460 km radius, 4,600 km long.
Obayashi, a Japanese builder, plans an 8-day climber trip to geosynchronous orbit, with a target date of 2050.

leo.who_owns: No country can own it. Each launched object is to be entered on the register of a launching country, and that country keeps legal power over the object and everyone on it. Countries are responsible for the private activity they license.
leo.hook: You cannot leave Earth without a launching country. Under the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, that country must give you permission (Article VI), register you and keep legal power over your station (Article VIII). A US citizen launching from anywhere outside the US needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the US aviation regulator (51 USC 50904).
leo.can_you_build: You would buy a launch from a licensed operator, which brings you under a national licensing system. Radio contact needs a filing with the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio coordination, through a member country. Supplies come from Earth, and crews on the International Space Station (ISS) still rely on delivered tanks, water and food. Asgardia's satellite claim is covered in its own separate entry.

rules.says: Space is free for all countries to use.
No country may take it over by claiming authority, by using or occupying it, or by any other means.
Countries answer for private space activities, which need permission and continuing oversight.
Launching countries are liable, meaning legally bound to pay, for damage.
The country that registers an object keeps legal power and control over it and anyone on board.
Countries must pay due attention to others and consult before causing harmful interference.
Under this treaty on listing space objects, the launching country registers each object and reports its details to the UN.
Under this treaty on who pays for space damage, a launching country must pay for damage on Earth or to aircraft whether or not it was at fault. Elsewhere it pays only if it was at fault.
Under the ITU's founding treaty, orbits and frequencies are limited natural resources, and stations must not cause harmful interference.

facts: Low Earth orbit is under 2,000 km above Earth, according to the European Space Agency.

The Outer Space Treaty had 118 member countries and 23 that had signed without joining as at 1 January 2026, up from 116 a year earlier with the addition of Latvia and Malaysia. The UN Office for Outer Space Affairs lists no later member.

The Registration Convention has 77 members. The Liability Convention has 100, plus 4 organizations that accept it by declaration. The Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts in distress, has 100, plus 3 declarations.
The ISS costs about $3 billion a year to operate, according to NASA's Inspector General.

stratosphere-near-space.who_owns: Over a country, this height is treated in practice as that country's airspace, and there is no agreed top to airspace. Over the high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, the same freedom applies as at lower heights. No treaty sets special rules for 'near space', the band above normal aircraft and below orbit.
stratosphere-near-space.hook: Article 1 of the Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, applies at whatever height a country can reach. The 2023 balloon incident shows that countries will act at balloon height. Launches and balloon flights also begin on a country's soil.
stratosphere-near-space.can_you_build: Balloons and high-altitude platforms need a launch site, an entry on a register and radio frequencies from a country. No self-governing station at this height has been found.

rules.says: Countries hold full authority over the air above their territory, and no height limit is stated.
Outer space cannot be taken over by any country, though the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on what countries may do in space, does not say where outer space begins.
The UN's space committee has considered where to draw the line between air and space since 1967 without agreeing, and some countries oppose defining a line at all.

Australia, Denmark and Kazakhstan use 100 km in their space laws, and the US has endorsed 100 km as the point where its Air Force's and Space Force's areas of responsibility divide, according to a 2025 UN submission. New Zealand defines high altitude as starting from flight level 600, an aviation measure of about 60,000 feet.

facts: The Kármán line at 100 km is a reference point that has not been agreed in law, according to the Library of Congress.
Other proposals include 110 km (UN paper A/AC.105/L.168, cited in the submission), and 120 km and 160 km for the top of near space.

Most aircraft fly below flight level 600, according to the Jakarta Post, citing the International Civil Aviation Organization. A UN submission puts flight level 600 at approximately 18 km, while the Jakarta Post says 20 km.

A UN submission states that national airspace has functionally not been legislated beyond 400,000 feet (about 122 km). That language comes from a draft treaty by the International Association for the Advancement of Space Safety, and it is not law.

airborne-habitats.who_owns: Air over a country falls under that country's rules, and no case of anyone claiming a flying nation has been found in the published descriptions. In practice, a platform answers to the aviation and radio authorities that certify it. The International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for radio coordination, treats a high-altitude platform as a radio station.
airborne-habitats.hook: Safety certification and flight permission before takeoff, radio frequency rules, and the need to land somewhere for maintenance. Stratobus, a planned airship platform, expects a couple of days on the ground each year.
airborne-habitats.can_you_build: Uncrewed platforms have flown, but no one lives on one. Sky Cruise is a video concept. Several programs ended: Facebook's Aquila drone was halted in 2018, Google's Loon balloons ended in 2021, and Titan Aerospace's Solara was shut down by 2017.

rules.says: Defines a high-altitude platform station as a radio station on an object at 20 to 50 km up, at a specified nominal fixed point relative to the Earth.
Class A, the controlled airspace used by airliners in the US, ends at 60,000 feet, and these platforms fly above it. The published FAA page does not say how they are regulated up there.

facts: The radio band for high-altitude platforms covers heights of 20 to 50 km.
Stratobus's 2015 design: about 20 km up, 100 m long, 5 tons, carrying 250 kg of equipment. It was described as 142 m long in 2025.
Helios, a NASA solar aircraft, reached 96,863 feet on 13 August 2001 and broke up in flight in 2003.
Airbus Zephyr, a solar drone, can fly for 64 days.

airspace-over-high-seas.name: Airspace over open ocean, coastal resource zones and Antarctica
airspace-over-high-seas.who_owns: No country holds full authority here. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, every country may fly over the high seas (open ocean outside any country's control) and over the exclusive economic zone or EEZ (the belt up to 200 nautical miles from a coast where the coastal country controls resources). Flight rules come from the standards of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency for civil flying. Over Antarctica, authority is unsettled because claims to the continent are frozen by treaty. These are the main exceptions to the common statement that the country below controls the air.
airspace-over-high-seas.hook: Registration and nationality. Articles 17 to 20 of the Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, tie each aircraft to one country, and that country applies its rules wherever the aircraft flies (Article 12). Every aircraft also has to take off and land somewhere.
airspace-over-high-seas.can_you_build: You can fly here with a registered aircraft. A self-governing craft that stayed permanently in the air would still need to be on a country's register, and without one it would have no right to enter any country's airspace.

rules.says: Every country is free to fly over the high seas.
The same freedom applies over the EEZ.
Rules for the deep seabed (called 'the Area') do not change the legal status of the air above it.
'Over the high seas, the rules in force shall be those established under this Convention.'
Piracy and boarding rules extend to aircraft: private aircraft may be seized for piracy, and military aircraft may stop and inspect a suspect ship, known as the right of visit.

The Antarctic Treaty, which governs the continent south of 60 degrees South, freezes claims. Countries that do not recognize a claim therefore appear able to dispute whether the air above a claimed sector counts as the claimant's airspace. This is an interpretation, because the treaty does not address authority over airspace.

facts: Common summaries say the country below owns the air. That leaves out four points: (1) no country holds authority over the high seas, about 58.6% of the sea surface; (2) Antarctica's airspace has no settled authority; (3) no treaty sets the upper limit of airspace; (4) an EEZ gives no airspace rights, and only the territorial sea, up to 12 nautical miles from the coast, does.

airspace-over-states.who_owns: The country below. Its authority over the air is complete and shuts out everyone else's, and its territory includes both land and coastal waters. No treaty sets how high that goes.
airspace-over-states.hook: Article 1 of the Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, gives the country this power directly. A country may require any aircraft to land. In February 2023, US jets shot down a Chinese balloon over American airspace. A flying platform that no country has registered appears to have no standing under Articles 17 to 20 of the treaty.
airspace-over-states.can_you_build: Only with the local country's permission and under its registration rules.

rules.says: Every country has complete and exclusive authority over the airspace above its territory.
Territory means land and the coastal waters next to it that are under a country's authority.
Scheduled international flights need permission from the country flown over or landed in.
Pilotless aircraft need special permission to fly over a country.
Each country enforces flight rules over its territory and for aircraft carrying its registration marks, wherever they are.
An aircraft has the nationality of the country that registered it, may be registered in one country only, under that country's law, and must display its marks.

Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a coastal country's authority also covers the air above its territorial sea, the belt of sea next to its coast.

facts: The International Civil Aviation Organization, the UN agency for civil flying, has 193 member countries, according to its own page.

ships-flag.who_owns: The flag state, meaning the country whose flag the ship flies and whose register lists it. On the high seas (open ocean outside any country's control), only that country has legal power over the ship, with limited exceptions, and each country sets its own conditions for granting its flag.
ships-flag.hook: A flag issued by a place no other country recognizes gives no protection. Under Article 110(1)(d) of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, the ship appears open to being treated as having no nationality and being boarded, although the treaty does not mention unrecognized flags. US law, for one, calls a vessel 'without nationality' in several situations and applies its drug law to such vessels (46 USC 70502). With a real flag, the limit is the flag state itself, which keeps legal power over everyone aboard.
ships-flag.can_you_build: This is the easy route: buy a ship and register it in a country that offers a register. You then live under that country's law on board, and it can remove you from its register. A ship can only be sovereign in the legal sense if a country stands behind it, which brings the project back to the need for recognition by other countries.

rules.says: Every country, including one with no coast, may sail ships under its flag.
Each country sets the conditions for its flag. There must be a 'genuine link' between the country and the ship.
A ship may fly one flag only. On the high seas, only the flag state has legal power over it, except in cases set by treaty or by UNCLOS.
A ship that uses two or more flags as it suits may be treated as having no nationality.
The flag state must keep a register and enforce rules on seaworthiness, crew and safety.
After a collision, only the flag state or the person's own country may bring criminal charges.
Each flag state must require ship captains to rescue people in danger at sea.
Any slave who reaches any ship, under any flag, is free by that fact.

A warship may board a foreign ship if it has reasonable grounds to suspect piracy, slave trading, unauthorized broadcasting (where its own country has power under Article 109), that the ship has no nationality, or that a ship flying a foreign flag or refusing to show one really has the warship's nationality. The ground that matters for self-declared flags is Article 110(1)(d), having no nationality.

facts: Full protection from boarding by other countries applies only to warships and government ships not used for trade (Articles 95 and 96).

high-seas.name: High seas (open ocean beyond 200 nautical miles, about 370 km)
high-seas.who_owns: No country owns it. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, the sea here is open to every country, and each ship answers to the country whose flag it flies. Article 87 words these freedoms as belonging to countries and does not grant them to private people.
high-seas.hook: Having no flag. A vessel with no flag country can be boarded under Article 110(1)(d). The article speaks of ships, so applying it to a fixed structure is an inference. The people on board also remain nationals of their home countries, and a country such as the US claims power to prosecute crimes committed by or against its nationals in 'any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation' (18 USC 7(7)).
high-seas.can_you_build: Physically, you would tow or sail a vessel or platform out and bring supplies from a port, which puts you under that port's law on each visit. Legally, you would register it with a willing country, which means accepting that country's law on board. Beyond 200 nautical miles, the seabed may still be part of another country's extended continental shelf (seabed a country controls beyond the usual limit, Article 76) or part of the deep seabed run by the International Seabed Authority, so anchoring raises separate questions.

rules.says: Applies the high-seas rules to all sea outside a country's exclusive economic zone (its coastal resource zone), its territorial sea (the belt next to its coast), its internal waters and the waters between the islands of an island nation.

The high seas are open to all countries. The listed freedoms include sailing, flying over, laying cables and building artificial islands, the last one 'subject to Part VI' (the continental shelf rules) and 'permitted under international law'.
No country may validly claim any part of the high seas as its own.
A ship sails under one flag only and answers to that flag country on the high seas.

A warship may board a foreign ship, other than a warship or government ship, if it has reasonable grounds to suspect piracy, slave trading, unauthorized broadcasting (where its own country has power under Article 109), that the ship has no nationality, or that a ship flying a foreign flag or refusing to show one really has the warship's nationality.

Since 17 January 2026, this treaty on protecting marine life covers areas outside any country's control. Its members must assess the environmental impact of planned activities under their control there before allowing them.

facts: About 58.6% of the sea surface is high seas, by the calculation of MarineRegions, a marine geography database.
Parliamentarians for Global Action puts the high seas at 43% of Earth's surface. Another advocacy page on the same site says 'about half'. The figures depend on the definition used.
The ocean covers more than 70% of Earth's surface, according to the US agency NOAA.
UNCLOS has 172 members and has been in effect since 16 November 1994. The United States is outside it, according to a briefing on seabed rules by the law firm A&O Shearman.

The BBNJ Agreement, the treaty on marine life in areas outside any country's control, was adopted on 19 June 2023 and took effect on 17 January 2026. It had 145 signing countries and 105 members on the UN status page in November 2026. Its first Conference of the Parties, the members' meeting, is set for 11 to 22 January 2027.

The BBNJ Agreement adds rules on genetic resources from sea life (no country may claim authority over them, Article 11), marine protected areas, environmental impact assessment and help for countries to build their capacity.

central-arctic-ocean-and-svalbard.who_owns: The central Arctic Ocean is high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, surrounded by the coastal resource zones of five countries. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, applies there. Svalbard, a group of Arctic islands, is Norwegian territory. The 1920 Svalbard Treaty confirms Norway's full authority and gives nationals of the other member countries equal rights to do business and gain access.
central-arctic-ocean-and-svalbard.hook: In the ocean, the same limits apply as on the high seas. On Svalbard, Norwegian law and the Governor, Norway's local official, apply. Although no visa is needed, Norway can refuse or expel people under its Svalbard regulations, including those without the means to support themselves there.
central-arctic-ocean-and-svalbard.can_you_build: On Svalbard, a foreigner needs no Norwegian visa or residence permit, and living there gives no rights to govern. In the central ocean, ice has generally covered the water all year, though it is shrinking, according to the opening text of the Central Arctic fisheries treaty.

rules.says: This fishing treaty covers the single area of high seas surrounded by Canada, Denmark/Greenland, Norway, Russia and the US. It runs for 16 years, with five-year renewals.

A coastal country's continental shelf, the seabed it controls for resources, can reach past 200 nautical miles within set limits. The seabed under the central Arctic can therefore belong to a coastal country and fall outside the international deep seabed.
Member countries recognize Norway's 'full and absolute sovereignty'.
Nationals of member countries have equal rights to fishing, hunting, access, trade and mining, subject to local law.
Taxes must be spent on Svalbard itself, and mining rules cannot favor anyone.
No naval base or fortification may be built.

facts: The Svalbard Treaty was signed on 9 February 1920 and has 49 members as of 2026, according to Wikipedia.
The fisheries agreement was concluded at Ilulissat, Greenland, on 3 October 2018 and took effect for Canada on 25 June 2021.
No official figure for the area of the Arctic high seas is given here.

floating-ice.who_owns: There is no settled answer. Legal writers take three views of an iceberg floating free. It belongs to no one (the Latin term is res nullius), it can be held under a claim by a country, or it is shared by all (res communis). Ice shelves around Antarctica, which are thick sheets of floating ice attached to land, fall inside the area of the Antarctic Treaty, which governs everything south of 60 degrees South.
floating-ice.hook: The supply line. No one needs to board the ice to stop a camp. Norway affected Camp Barneo, a temporary camp on Arctic ice, by restricting flights from Svalbard. How a court treated a killing on drifting ice is covered in the separate entry on Fletcher's Ice Island T-3.
floating-ice.can_you_build: Yes for weeks or years, but never permanently. Camp Barneo was rebuilt from scratch every April because the ice moves. Soviet and Russian research stations usually ran two or three years on one ice floe, and since the mid-2000s several were evacuated early because the ice thawed too fast. Max Perutz warned in 1942 that natural icebergs have too little surface above water for an airstrip and can roll over.

rules.says: The treaty covers everything south of 60 degrees South, including all ice shelves, without taking away rights any country has on the high seas in that area.

A 2022 article in the law journal Ius Novum argues that an iceberg floating free in Antarctic waters is no country's property and sits on the high seas, so taking and towing it would probably not breach any country's territorial rights.

rules.cite: Flag of the ship (see ships-flag zone)
rules.says: A towing ship answers to the country whose flag it flies. The same article notes that the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has joined neither the Antarctic Treaty System nor the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, which leaves open how far those rules bind a UAE-flagged tow.

facts: A23a, a giant iceberg, measured about 3,500 km2 in January 2025 and 180 km2 by March 2026.
North Pole-1, a Soviet station on drifting ice, ran for 9 months and drifted 2,850 km in 1937-38.
Some 800 people have drifted on North Pole stations since 1937.
A visit to Barneo cost from about $20,000, and a drift of 0.8 km per hour was recorded in 2007.
Project Habakkuk, a plan for a ship built of pykrete (ice mixed with wood pulp), had a planned length of 600 m, and the pykrete needed cooling to -16 C.
The UAE Iceberg Project, a plan to tow an iceberg to the Emirates, was estimated at $100-150 million.

new-land.who_owns: Almost always the country whose waters the ground rises in, because that country already holds the seabed there. Land that rises from a seabed no one holds has only one tested case, Graham Island off Sicily in 1831, and it sank before anyone's claim succeeded. Land built by people has weaker legal status than land made by nature.
new-land.hook: Governments reach new ground within days. In 1831, a Sicilian customs official landed on Graham Island by 17 July and a British captain by 2 August. In 1963, Iceland immediately answered a joke French claim on the new island of Surtsey, and the country then closed the island to almost everyone.
new-land.can_you_build: In practice, no. New ash and silt wash away. Graham Island lasted about six months, Zalzala Koh about three years, and the merged Hunga island seven. Surtsey, which did harden, is a nature reserve where only a few scientists may land.

rules.says: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, an island is land that formed naturally, has water all round it, and stays above water at high tide.
Rocks that cannot support people living there or an economy of their own get no exclusive economic zone (coastal resource zone) or continental shelf (seabed rights).
A coastal country holds full authority over its territorial sea, the belt of sea next to its coast, and the seabed below it, so a volcano that surfaces there rises on ground it already holds.
Artificial islands are not islands in law. They get no territorial sea and do not move any sea boundary.

rules.cite: Bay of Bengal Maritime Boundary Arbitration (Bangladesh v India), 2014
rules.says: An arbitration tribunal, a panel of judges chosen to settle a dispute, drew the sea boundary and left the site of the vanished island of South Talpatti on the Indian side.

facts: Graham Island, 1831: about 4 km2 and 63 m high at its peak, gone by January 1832.
Surtsey, Iceland: the eruption began on 14 November 1963 and ended on 5 June 1967, when its highest point was 174 m.
Hunga Tonga and Hunga Haʻapai, in Tonga, joined in 2015 and were mostly destroyed in January 2022, leaving small remnants.
South Talpatti, in the Bay of Bengal, appeared after the November 1970 cyclone, never rose above 2 m and was gone around March 2010.
Zalzala Koh rose on 24 September 2013, about 2 km offshore, and was gone by the end of 2016.
Fonuafoʻou appeared on 14 October 1885, collapsed in 1949, and is now 17 m under water.

eez-shelf.name: Exclusive economic zone and continental shelf (a coastal country's resource zone, 12 to 200 nautical miles out, sometimes further)
eez-shelf.who_owns: The nearest coastal country. The exclusive economic zone (EEZ) is the belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles (about 370 km) from the coast. The continental shelf is the seabed extending out from that coast. The country does not own the water outright, but it holds the rights to the resources and the exclusive right to authorize artificial islands and certain installations there. Other countries remain free to sail and fly through.
eez-shelf.hook: Under Article 60 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, an artificial island needs the coastal country's permission. So does an installation with an economic purpose or one that could interfere with that country's rights. Its tax and immigration laws then apply there. In 2019, Thailand's navy raided a floating home off Phuket, which its owners said was anchored just over 12 nautical miles from shore. The navy said the owners had endangered national sovereignty, an offense punishable by life imprisonment or death.
eez-shelf.can_you_build: You can sail through freely. To stay on a fixed structure, you need the coastal country's permission, which puts you under its law by treaty. This appears to rule out an independent project here unless the coastal country agrees to carve out a special zone.

rules.says: The coastal country has rights over the resources in a zone up to 200 nautical miles from its baselines, the lines from which sea zones are measured, usually the low-tide coast.
The coastal country has the exclusive right to build and to authorize artificial islands, and installations with economic purposes or that could interfere with its rights.
It has exclusive legal power over such structures, including customs, tax, health, safety and immigration law.
Artificial islands are not islands in law. They have no territorial sea of their own and do not change any sea boundary.
Safety zones around structures may reach 500 metres at most, unless international standards allow more.
Rights over seabed resources on the continental shelf do not depend on occupying it, and Article 60 applies equally to structures on the shelf.
Other countries keep the freedom to sail, fly and lay cables in the EEZ, and must pay due attention to the coastal country's rights.
The coastal country may board and arrest to enforce its fishing rules, and may chase a ship out to sea, known as hot pursuit, for violations in the zone.

facts: The 230 EEZs cover 136,850,878 km² in total, excluding joint arrangements and overlapping claims, according to a Flanders Marine Institute poster using 2019 data.
The largest EEZ on that poster is Russia's at 7,734,809 km², followed by Australia's at 6,871,622 km².
The US EEZ covers more than 3.4 million square nautical miles, according to the US agency NOAA.

territorial-sea.name: Territorial sea (the belt next to the coast, up to 12 nautical miles or about 22 km)
territorial-sea.who_owns: The coastal country has full authority over the water, the seabed under it and the air above it, the same as over its land. It exercises this subject to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, and other international law (Article 2(3)). The main limit is foreign ships' right of innocent passage, meaning the right to pass through peacefully and without delay.
territorial-sea.hook: Ordinary national law applies, because you are inside the country. A country can also move the line. The UK extended its territorial waters to 12 nautical miles in 1987, which put Sealand, a self-declared state on an old sea fort about 11 to 13 km offshore, in waters recognized as British.
territorial-sea.can_you_build: Only with the coastal country's permission and under its law. Any structure here is a domestic building project.

rules.says: A coastal country's authority extends to the territorial sea, its seabed and the air above it.
A country may set a territorial sea of up to 12 nautical miles from its baselines, the lines from which sea zones are measured.
The normal baseline is the low-water line on the country's official charts.
Offshore installations and artificial islands do not count as harbour works and do not push the boundary out.

Foreign ships may pass through if the passage does not harm peace, order or security. Staying put to set up a settlement appears to fall outside what passage covers, on a reading of Articles 18 and 19.
Submarines must travel on the surface and show their flag here.
In a further belt out to 24 nautical miles, the country may act to prevent and punish customs, tax, immigration and health offenses committed in its territory or territorial sea.

facts: 12 nautical miles is about 22 km.
Sealand sits about 6 to 7 nautical miles off the English coast, according to Wikipedia.

reefs-low-tide-elevations.name: Reefs, rocks and land that shows only at low tide
reefs-low-tide-elevations.who_owns: It depends on where the feature sits and whether it stays dry at high tide. A feature covered at high tide, called a low-tide elevation, cannot be claimed by occupying it, according to the 2016 South China Sea tribunal, a panel of judges set up under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans. It belongs to whichever legal zone it lies in.
reefs-low-tide-elevations.hook: The tribunal's test looks at a feature's natural state, so dredging sand onto it cannot create a claim. The nearest country also has a practical remedy. Tonga claimed the Minerva Reefs in the Pacific on 24 February 1972, about five weeks after a group declared a state called Minerva there. Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Nauru and Samoa backed Tonga, which sent an expedition that arrived on 18 June 1972.
reefs-low-tide-elevations.can_you_build: Building on a shallow reef is physically possible, as Minerva's founders showed by bringing in sand from Australia by barge in 1971. Legally, it creates no territorial sea or exclusive economic zone (Article 60(8)). Safety zones of up to 500 m are set by the coastal country and not by the builder (Article 60(4)-(5)), and if the reef is inside a country's exclusive economic zone, that country must authorize the work under Article 60.

rules.says: An island is naturally formed land, surrounded by water and above water at high tide.

Rocks that cannot support human habitation or an economic life of their own get no exclusive economic zone (coastal resource zone) or continental shelf (seabed rights). They still get a territorial sea, a belt of coastal water, of up to 12 nautical miles under Article 121(2)-(3) and Article 3.
A low-tide elevation is natural land that is above water only at low tide. If it is more than 12 nautical miles from land, it has no territorial sea of its own.
Filling in a reef makes an artificial island, which generates no territorial sea.

Mischief Reef, Second Thomas Shoal and Subi Reef are low-tide elevations and are 'not features that are capable of appropriation by occupation or otherwise'. A feature's status depends on its natural condition, before any building.

facts: Minerva's declaration was made on 19 January 1972. In 1982, a group trying to reoccupy the reef was forced off by Tongan troops after three weeks, according to Wikipedia.
The tribunal found that no feature in the Spratly Islands can generate an exclusive economic zone, and that they cannot do so collectively as a unit.

abandoned-platforms.who_owns: The law of the place applies, along with the rights of whoever owns the structure. An abandoned platform in a country's exclusive economic zone (the belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles from its coast where it controls resources) stays under that country's sole legal power. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, requires disused structures to be removed.
abandoned-platforms.hook: The coastal country's legal power under Article 60, plus property and trespass law where the owner is a company or government. Sealand's fort stood outside British waters until the UK extended them in 1987. Rose Island, a platform built on purpose off Rimini, Italy, was taken over by Italian officers 56 days after declaring independence, and the Italian Navy bombed it in 1969.
abandoned-platforms.can_you_build: Boarding is physically possible, but it gives you little legal standing. Oil platforms stand on a continental shelf, the seabed a coastal country controls, so they normally fall under that country's power through Articles 60 and 80. Buying a structure from its owner would appear to transfer ownership only, because legal power under Article 60 belongs to the country.

rules.says: Abandoned or disused installations must be removed to keep shipping safe, and any remains must be made public.
The coastal country's legal power covers installations in its exclusive economic zone and on its continental shelf.
A platform has no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has, so it cannot be the base of a claim to the water around it.
Offshore installations are not part of the coast when boundaries are drawn.
This treaty on dumping treats all dumping at sea as prohibited unless explicitly permitted.

facts: Rose Island: independence was declared on 1 May 1968, Italian officers took control on 26 June 1968, and the navy bombed it twice, the second time on 13 February 1969.
Roughs Tower, the fort that became Sealand, was built by Britain in 1943 and sunk in place on a sandbar, according to Wikipedia.

disputed-islands.who_owns: Several countries claim them at once and keep armed garrisons there. A newcomer would be one more claimant facing armed occupiers. The 2016 South China Sea tribunal, a panel of judges set up under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, ruled on sea zones and said it does not rule on any question of who holds authority over land territory.
disputed-islands.hook: Armed force on site and the coastal countries' navies, with the practical limit being whichever of them holds the nearest feature. Because a feature's legal status depends on its natural condition, engineering work gains no legal ground.
disputed-islands.can_you_build: Practically out of reach, since the islands are garrisoned by rival claimants, as shown in Wikipedia's table of who occupies what. Tomás Cloma's 1956 'Free Territory of Freedomland' claim is covered in its own separate entry.

rules.says: Rocks that cannot support human habitation or an economic life of their own get no exclusive economic zone (coastal resource zone) or continental shelf (seabed rights).

No feature in the Spratly Islands can generate an exclusive economic zone, individually or as a group. The tribunal found no legal basis for China to claim historic rights to resources inside the nine-dash line, the line China uses for its claims in the South China Sea.
China's land-building at seven features caused severe harm to coral and violated its duties, and it built on Mischief Reef inside the Philippines' exclusive economic zone.
Land-building creates no new territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that natural land has.

facts: The Spratlys have 177 hectares of natural island area, or about 200 hectares counting reclaimed land, in the table used by Wikipedia.
The Paracels are more than 30 islands, under Chinese control in practice since 1974, according to Wikipedia.
The award was issued on 12 July 2016 by a tribunal under Annex VII of UNCLOS. It is final and binding on the parties to the case under Article 296. China took no part in the proceedings.

undersea-water-column.who_owns: It follows the zone at the surface above it. Under the high seas (open ocean outside any country's control), the water itself is high seas, and the bottom is either a coastal country's continental shelf (seabed it controls) or 'the Area', the deep seabed run by the International Seabed Authority (ISA). Being underwater does not create a separate legal space.
undersea-water-column.hook: The same limits apply as at the surface. Under Article 110 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, the rule on boarding a vessel with no flag still applies to a submarine, though a warship has to find it first. Any anchor on the seabed appears to give the coastal country, where it sits on that country's shelf, a physical point of contact.
undersea-water-column.can_you_build: Moving habitats would likely count as vessels and need a flag. Fixed habitats on a continental shelf need the coastal country's permission where Article 60 applies. On the deep seabed, taking any part as your own is barred, and the ISA's rules on installations are written for mining. The treaty gives no clear answer on whether a stationary habitat tethered to the seabed counts as a ship or an installation, and the question appears open.

rules.says: High-seas freedoms apply to the water, so a submerged vessel under a flag appears to be treated as a ship, although UNCLOS does not define 'ship'.
In the territorial sea, the belt next to a coast, submarines must travel on the surface and show a flag.

Article 60 applies on the continental shelf (Article 80), so artificial islands, and installations with an economic purpose or that could interfere with the coastal country's rights, fall under the coastal country.
Article 137 bars anyone from taking any part of the deep seabed. Article 147 applies ISA rules to installations used for mining, so it does not appear to clearly reach a habitat with no mining.
Research installations follow the rules of the zone where they sit, have no island status, and get safety zones of 500 m at most.

facts: The seafloor reaches more than 8 km deep in the Mariana Trench, according to the ISA.
Safety zones around research installations are 500 m at most (Article 260).

deep-seabed-area.name: Deep ocean floor, 'the Area' (run by the International Seabed Authority)
deep-seabed-area.who_owns: Nobody can own it. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, the seabed beyond countries' continental shelves and its minerals are the 'common heritage of mankind', meaning they belong to humanity as a whole. The International Seabed Authority (ISA), based in Jamaica, controls mineral activities on behalf of all. The water above remains high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control.
deep-seabed-area.hook: Article 137 says no claim to any part of it will be recognized. An operator also needs a sponsoring country (Article 153), a country that takes responsibility for the operator, so a self-declared country cannot sponsor itself. A rival US route exists through the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980. Under that law, the US agency NOAA found the application of The Metals Company's US subsidiary to be in 'substantial compliance' on 9 March 2026. The ISA's commission is investigating whether that breaches contractors' duties.
deep-seabed-area.can_you_build: You can visit by submersible. Anything related to mining needs a sponsoring country and an ISA contract. The rules for exploitation, meaning commercial mining, were still unfinished after the July 2026 session of the ISA Council, which asked its staff for a roadmap and a new negotiating text.

rules.says: The Area and its resources are the common heritage of mankind.
No country may claim authority over any part of it, no country or person may take any part of it as their own, and no such claim or taking will be recognized.
Rights in the resources belong to humanity as a whole. Minerals can be sold only under ISA rules.
This set of rules leaves the legal status of the water and air above unchanged.
The Area is open to use for peaceful purposes only.
Installations used for mineral activities in the Area must be placed and removed under ISA rules, and they cannot have a territorial sea (the text says they 'do not possess the status of islands').
Archaeological and historical objects found there are to be preserved or disposed of for the benefit of humanity.
Operators need sponsorship from a member country and an approved plan of work.
The ISA is the body through which member countries control activities in the Area, and all UNCLOS members belong to it.

facts: The ISA's area covers about 54% of the total area of the world's oceans, by its own figure.
The ISA had 172 members as of 6 February 2026, made up of 171 countries plus the European Union.

The ISA lists 15-year exploration contracts with 22 contractors. Its text counts 19 contracts for nodules (mineral lumps on the seabed), 7 for sulphides and 5 for crusts, 31 in all. Its sulphide sub-count adds up to 8, so the page is not fully consistent.

Only exploration is allowed so far. The March 2026 Council approved no commercial mining, and the Mining Code, the planned set of commercial rules, remained unfinished. The July 2026 draft decision says commercial mining should not take place without rules.
The US has not joined the UNCLOS deep-sea mining system, according to the law firm A&O Shearman.

underground-subseabed.who_owns: Whoever holds the surface above. A country's authority runs down from its land and from its territorial sea, the belt of sea next to its coast. Past that, a coastal country keeps rights in the rock below its continental shelf, the seabed extending out from its coast, and it can tunnel there at any depth of water. A private landowner may own the ground below, though in many places minerals beyond a set depth belong to the government.
underground-subseabed.hook: Ordinary police, fire and licensing law. A bunker has an address, so officials can simply enter it. The local Dutch town refused CyberBunker, a web-hosting business in a former military bunker, a business licence after a 2002 fire. German investigators tapped its internet traffic under a warrant from 2015, and 600 police raided its second bunker in 2019.
underground-subseabed.can_you_build: Yes, as private property under local law. Buying the land is the easy part: Survival Condo paid $300,000 for a former missile silo. Geology and safety rules still apply. Vivos, a bunker developer, dropped its largest project in 2014 over the stability of a former mine. Going deep underground does not change which country you are in.

rules.says: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a coastal country's authority reaches the seabed and the rock beneath it in its territorial sea.

The continental shelf is the seabed and the rock beneath it beyond the territorial sea, out to the edge of the continental margin (where the continent's underwater slope ends) or to 200 nautical miles.
The coastal country alone may explore the shelf and take its resources, and nobody else may do so without its express consent, even if it never uses them.
The shelf rules do not limit a coastal country's right to exploit the rock below by tunnelling, however deep the water above.
Whoever owns the soil owns up to the sky and down to the depths, as an old legal saying puts it. Modern law keeps a limited form of this and often separates mineral rights from ownership of the land.

facts: The CyberBunker site at Kloetinge, the Netherlands: 20,000 square feet, built in 1955, bought in 1995.
Pionen, a data centre in central Stockholm: 1,100 m2 under 30 m of granite.
Survival Condo: a silo 197 feet deep, with 15 floors and 12 units, costing about $20 million by 2012.
Vivos: 575 bunkers at the former Black Hills Ordnance Depot in South Dakota.
Vivos at Atchison, Kansas: planned for 5,000 people in a former mine of 2,700,000 square feet, and cancelled in June 2014.

inland-waters.who_owns: The countries around the water. A border lake or river is divided by a treaty, and where a treaty only names a river, the line usually follows the thalweg, meaning the deepest channel. A few waters have no agreed line at all, and they still belong to the countries on the shore, never to a newcomer.
inland-waters.hook: Lake police and customs officers from the nearest shore. On Migingo, a tiny island in Lake Victoria, Uganda sold special permits to residents and posted 48 police officers. Caspian Sea patrol boats have fired on survey vessels.
inland-waters.can_you_build: Only with the permission of the country that holds the spot. A treaty you did not sign can reassign a river island, as the Treaty of Lausanne did to Ada Kaleh in the Danube in 1923, and a dam can drown it, as happened there in 1970. On Pheasant Island, between France and Spain, access itself is forbidden.

rules.cite: Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea (2018)
rules.says: This treaty on the Caspian Sea was not in force as of September 2026, because all five shore countries must ratify it (formally approve it) and Iran has not. It would give each shore country 15 nautical miles (about 28 km) of territorial water and a further 10 nautical miles (about 19 km) of exclusive fishing. The rest of the surface would be a common space open to the five members, and the seabed is left to agreements between the countries concerned.
Pheasant Island in the Bidasoa river stays a condominium, meaning France and Spain share it. Each governs it for six months in turn.
Where an 1890 treaty named the 'main channel' of the Chobe river, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, worked out which channel that was. The island fell on the Botswana side.

rules.cite: Kenya Colony and Protectorate Order in Council (1926)
rules.says: A colonial order draws the Kenya-Uganda line across Lake Victoria by straight lines between named islands. It is copied into the Ugandan constitution and was used to place Migingo in 2009.
No binding agreement fixes the borders in the deep part of the lake. Areas under 25 m deep go to the nearest country, and shipping and fishing have treaties of their own.

facts: The Caspian Sea covers 389,000 km2 and has five shore countries.

The Caspian convention was signed on 12 August 2018 at Aktau, Kazakhstan. It provides for 15 nautical miles (about 28 km) of territorial water plus 10 nautical miles (about 19 km) of exclusive fishing, and it was not in force as of September 2026.
Pheasant Island in January 2018 measured about 200 m by 40 m. It is uninhabited and eroding.
Migingo covers about 2,000 m2, with 131 people reported in 2009. Ugandan police estimated about 500.
Migingo lies 510 m on the Kenyan side of the line, according to a 2009 survey whose report was still unpublished in January 2025.
Sedudu, also called Kasikili, covers about 5 km2 and is flooded for several months each year.

terra-nullius-land.who_owns: Bir Tawil, on the Egypt-Sudan border: neither Egypt nor Sudan claims it, because each prefers a different border that gives it the more valuable Halaib Triangle. Gornja Siga, on the Danube: Croatia and Serbia dispute where the border lies, and Croatia controls access on the ground.
terra-nullius-land.hook: Occupation in the classic legal sense is something countries do, so an individual's flag appears not to be enough, on a reading of paragraph 79 of the Western Sahara opinion of the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court. The neighbors' border law then becomes the practical limit. Croatian police have detained and fined people entering Gornja Siga, one was sentenced to 15 days in prison, and makeshift buildings were removed in September 2023. Bir Tawil can be reached only through Egypt or Sudan. People also use Bir Tawil, including the Ababda people, according to a paper cited by Wikipedia.
terra-nullius-land.can_you_build: Bir Tawil is land between Egypt and Sudan, so entry is through one of them. Gornja Siga is forest on the Danube that can be reached only by crossing Croatian or Serbian border controls, and it is subject to Croatian policing. Permanent settlement has not been achieved at either.

rules.says: 'Terra nullius' is Latin for land belonging to no one, which can be acquired by occupying it. It is a technical legal term for how countries acquire land.

The practice of countries at the relevant time did not treat land inhabited by tribes or peoples with social and political organization as terra nullius, and the Court applied that to Western Sahara's nomadic peoples.

The Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty whose definition of a state is the usual checklist, says a state needs a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter relations with other states.
A state's political existence does not depend on recognition by others.
General international law contains no applicable ban on declarations of independence. This is a narrow point, and the Court did not say that a declaration creates a state.

facts: Bir Tawil covers 2,060 km², according to Wikipedia.
It exists because of two boundaries: a straight political line of 1899 and an irregular administrative line of 1902.
Gornja Siga covers about 7 km². The border was drawn by a 1947 commission whose conclusions were never made law, according to the Italian newspaper Il Post.
The 2015 claim to Gornja Siga known as Liberland attracted hundreds of thousands of citizenship applications, according to Vice.

Whether Gornja Siga truly belongs to no one is contested. Both countries treat it as a border dispute, which is different from giving it up. The statements of the Croatian and Serbian foreign ministries themselves are not quoted here.

antarctica-unclaimed.who_owns: No country has claimed it, and the Antarctic Treaty, which governs the continent south of 60 degrees South, bars any new claim while it is in force. It is the largest unclaimed land on Earth.
antarctica-unclaimed.hook: The same limits apply as in the claimed sectors. An individual from a country outside the treaty is still a national of some country, and most routes pass through the territory of a treaty member. The United States and Russia say they keep the right to make claims later, according to Wikipedia, which marks one of the two statements as needing a citation.
antarctica-unclaimed.can_you_build: Wikipedia calls it remote even by Antarctic standards. Getting there means an expedition from the territory of a treaty member. Westarctica's claim is covered in its own separate entry.

rules.says: 'No new claim, or enlargement of an existing claim' may be asserted while the treaty is in force. The treaty binds its members. It says that no acts during the treaty can create rights of authority over the land, and applying that to acts by someone outside the treaty is an interpretation.
Expeditions must be notified by the member country they come from.
The environmental principles, ban on mining and impact assessment rules of the Madrid Protocol, an add-on to the Antarctic Treaty that protects the environment, apply here too.

facts: The area is 1,610,000 km², including the Eights Coast, according to Wikipedia.
The unclaimed sector runs from 90°W to 150°W. Norway's Peter I Island, at about 90°35'W, lies inside that band.

antarctica-claimed.who_owns: Seven countries claim sectors of the continent, and most others do not recognize those claims. The Antarctic Treaty, which governs the continent south of 60 degrees South, freezes the argument: claims are neither given up nor strengthened, and nothing done now can create a new one.
antarctica-claimed.hook: Each treaty member must give advance notice of expeditions by its ships or nationals and of those organized in or leaving from its territory (Article VII(5)). Members of the Madrid Protocol, an add-on to the treaty that protects the environment, must also assess the environmental impact of those activities (Article 8(2)). So the country of your passport or your departure port is the practical limit. Claimant countries may treat a sector as theirs, while other members are free not to recognize that (Article IV(1)(c)).
antarctica-claimed.can_you_build: If you leave from a treaty member's territory, that member must notify the other members, and an impact assessment applies if it has joined the Madrid Protocol. No rights of authority over the land can come from settling there (Article IV(2)). The treaty does not address private ownership of land.

rules.says: Peaceful purposes only, with no military bases or military exercises.
No member gives up or loses its claim or position.
Acts or activities while the treaty is in force cannot support or deny a claim to authority or 'create any rights of sovereignty', and no new claim may be asserted.
The treaty applies south of 60 degrees South, including ice shelves, and rights on the high seas in the area remain.
Members must give advance notice of all expeditions organized by their nationals or from their territory.
Any activity relating to mineral resources, other than science, is banned.
Activities need an environmental impact assessment beforehand.
Any Consultative Party, one of the decision-making members, can call a review conference once 50 years have passed since the protocol took effect.

facts: Antarctica covers 14,200,000 km², according to Wikipedia.
The claimants are Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway and the UK, making eight claims, according to Wikipedia.
The treaty has 58 members, of which 29 are Consultative (decision-making) and 29 Non-Consultative, according to its Secretariat.
The treaty has been in force since 23 June 1961 and the protocol since 14 January 1998, so by simple arithmetic the 50-year review point falls in January 2048.

inside-state.who_owns: The country whose borders it sits inside. Declaring independence changes nothing in that country's law, and its courts apply its tax and criminal law to you as usual.
inside-state.hook: Ordinary tax, planning and criminal law. The founder of Hutt River, a self-declared principality in Australia, was prosecuted over tax documents, and the courts held that declaring secession did not remove him from tax law.
inside-state.can_you_build: Buy land, or declare on land you already use. Nothing stops the declaration itself. Whether the government then acts appears to depend on whether the project costs it anything.

rules.says: The Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty whose definition of a state is the usual checklist, says a state needs a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter relations with other states.
A state's political existence does not depend on recognition by others. The practical tests still have to be met, on land that another state does not hold.

host-state-carve-outs.who_owns: The host country keeps full authority unless it gives the land away by treaty, and what one legislature grants, a later court or legislature may take back. Vatican City and the Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic status, show the rare end of the range. Honduras's ZEDEs, special zones exempt from local laws and taxes, show the common outcome.
host-state-carve-outs.hook: The host country's constitution and the next election. Investors may turn to treaty arbitration, where a panel of arbitrators decides a dispute between an investor and a country. Honduras Próspera Inc. brought a claim before ICSID, the World Bank body that hears such disputes. The claim was originally $10.775 billion and, according to Honduras's Attorney General, has dropped to $1.63 billion.
host-state-carve-outs.can_you_build: Among the routes to a new territory, this appears to be the only one with a working track record for a charter-style city, a city run under its own special rules, because it starts with a country's consent. It requires negotiating with a government and accepting its final authority.

rules.says: Declared unconstitutional the legal basis of ZEDEs, zones exempt from local laws and taxes, according to Reuters.
The Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church, is a non-member observer state at the UN, alongside the State of Palestine.

Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, a coastal country may authorize artificial islands and installations in its exclusive economic zone (coastal resource zone), so this route appears able to work at sea as well, on that country's terms.
A 2017 deal for a floating city, later dropped, according to sources listed in Wikipedia and the Minnesota Journal of Law, Science and Technology.

facts: In the ZEDE case, Próspera sits on Roatán, an island off the Honduran coast.
The claim was reduced by about 85%, according to the Honduran Attorney General's office as reported by Revista E&N.

The Sovereign Order of Malta describes itself as sovereign and conducts diplomatic relations, and it reported relations with 111 countries in 2021. The Lateran Treaty, on Vatican City, and the Fort St Angelo agreement were not reviewed for this entry.

unrecognised-state.who_owns: Disputed. A recognised country holds legal title, while a local government actually runs the place, usually after a war or with the army of a powerful backer.
unrecognised-state.hook: Force by the recognised country, as Azerbaijan used in Artsakh, an ethnic Armenian breakaway government, in 2023. Other countries' refusal of recognition also cuts access to treaties, banks and UN bodies.
unrecognised-state.can_you_build: Not by purchase. All the current cases came out of collapse, war or foreign protection.

rules.says: The Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty whose definition of a state is the usual checklist, sets four practical tests: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other states. Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia, is often cited as meeting them while lacking recognition.
Called Northern Cyprus's declaration legally invalid and asked UN members not to recognise it, an example of how the UN Security Council can keep a place out.

buffer-zones.who_owns: The surrounding countries or the parties to a ceasefire keep their claims. A peacekeeping force or ceasefire body controls entry.
buffer-zones.hook: Soldiers and entry permits control access. In the Korean zone, only two villages are allowed to remain. Chernobyl's exclusion zone in Ukraine is cordoned off, and the people who moved back live there without official permission.
buffer-zones.can_you_build: No declared state in such a zone has been found. People live in them as earlier residents or their descendants, and they remain citizens of an existing country.

rules.says: Each side moved back 2,000 metres from the front line, creating a zone about 4 km wide.
Patrolled by the UN force in Cyprus and extended after the 16 August 1974 ceasefire.

facts: The Cyprus zone covers 346 km² and runs 180 km, with about 10,000 residents.
The Korean Demilitarized Zone is about 250 km long by 4 km wide. The village of Tae Sung Dong had 218 people in 2008.
About 1,200 people returned to Chernobyl in 1986, and 135 remained in 2017.

buy-from-a-state.who_owns: The selling country holds authority over the land until a treaty moves it to the buyer.
buy-from-a-state.hook: The government that holds the land can refuse to sell, as Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly done. A buyer that is not a country has no treaty partner to hand authority over.
