buy-from-a-state.can_you_build: You would open talks with a government willing to give up authority over part of its land. The only private attempt confirmed so far, by Anton Bakov and his Romanov Empire project, reported unsuccessful talks with Kiribati and the Gambia as of 2017.

rules.says: Lists transfers of authority over territory by agreement in which money was paid, and every buyer and seller listed is a country or a country-like ruler. Leases are excluded.
The decision on Greenland's independence belongs to the Greenlandic people, followed by negotiation with Denmark and a referendum in Greenland.

facts: Alaska: $7.2 million in 1867, 1,717,856 km².
Louisiana: $15 million in 1803, 2,140,000 km².
Danish West Indies: $25 million in 1916, 400 km².
The latest purchase on the list is Gwadar, for £3 million in 1958.

leases-and-extraterritorial-spots.who_owns: The host country usually keeps final authority. Another country or body runs the place under a lease, a treaty or a diplomatic rule.
leases-and-extraterritorial-spots.hook: The host can end a lease with a fixed term, or the occupant can invite the police in, as Ecuador did at its London embassy in 2019. Airports stay under national law throughout, so staying in one gives no separate status.
leases-and-extraterritorial-spots.can_you_build: In the known cases, a lease has been granted only to a country or a country-like body. A private person can reach this kind of place only as a guest of that body, as someone seeking asylum in an embassy or as a stranded traveller.

rules.cite: Treaty between Malta and the Order of Malta, 1998
rules.says: Gives the Order of Malta land and buildings at Fort St Angelo in Malta, with listed privileges and legal protections, for 99 years. Either side may give notice in the 50th or 75th year, and the end of the agreement takes effect five years later.

rules.cite: 1934 US–Cuba Treaty of Relations, Article III
rules.says: Ending the Guantanamo Bay lease needs consent from both sides or full US military withdrawal.
These zones are fully under the legal power of the country where they sit, and local law applies inside them.

facts: Guantanamo Bay: 117 km², rent of $4,085 a year, with one cheque cashed since 1959.
New Territories, Hong Kong: leased for 99 years, rent-free, including 235 islands. The lease expired on 30 June 1997.
Panama Canal Zone: 1,432 km², from 1903 to 1979.
Julian Assange spent nearly seven years inside a suite of rooms in a London block of flats, the Ecuadorian embassy.
Mehran Nasseri, a stranded traveller, spent about 18 years in Terminal 1 of a Paris airport.

run-by-international-agreement.who_owns: Whoever the treaty names: the League of Nations (the body before the UN), the UN Security Council, a committee of foreign powers, or two countries jointly.
run-by-international-agreement.hook: These places exist only while the powers that signed keep agreeing. Danzig was annexed in 1939, Trieste was split in 1954, Tangier was abolished by its protecting powers, and the plan for Jerusalem was never carried out.
run-by-international-agreement.can_you_build: A person cannot start one. It takes a treaty or a UN decision, usually as a way to settle a dispute between countries after a war.

rules.says: In this peace treaty after World War I, Article 100 took Danzig from Germany, and Article 102 made it a Free City under League of Nations protection.

rules.cite: UN Security Council Resolution 16 and the 1947 Treaty of Peace with Italy
rules.says: Set up the Free Territory of Trieste under Security Council responsibility.
Placed Kosovo under UN administration from 1999.

facts: Tangier, Morocco: 373 km², from 1923 to 1956.
Danzig: 1,952 km², with 366,730 people in 1923.
Trieste lasted seven years and never received its governor.
Brčko District, Bosnia and Herzegovina: 493 km², 83,516 people, created on 8 March 2000.

secession-and-decolonisation.name: Breaking away by referendum or at the end of colonial rule
secession-and-decolonisation.who_owns: The existing country, unless it agrees to let go or loses control.
secession-and-decolonisation.hook: The parent country can refuse consent, send police or soldiers, take over the regional government or fight a war. Without its consent, recognition from other countries tends to stay limited.
secession-and-decolonisation.can_you_build: Win a popular mandate inside the territory, then get the parent country to agree to a binding vote. South Sudan, Montenegro and Eritrea all voted under agreed terms and were widely accepted afterwards.

rules.says: This treaty, whose definition of a state is the usual checklist, says a state needs a defined territory, a permanent population, a government and the capacity to deal with other states.

rules.cite: International Court of Justice, Kosovo advisory opinion, 22 July 2010
rules.says: The UN's top court found by 10 votes to 4 that Kosovo's declaration of independence did not violate international law.
Suspended Catalonia's referendum law and later declared it void.

facts: A count of Wikipedia's referendum table as it stood in November 2026: of about 123 votes counted, 31 led to a recognised independent state, 12 to control on the ground with no or partial recognition, 16 to a yes vote with no independence, and 59 to a no vote.
South Sudan: 98.83% voted yes.
Eritrea: 99.83% voted yes.
Montenegro: 55.5% voted yes, against a required 55%.

taking-over-a-state-or-town.who_owns: The existing country or local government. This route tries to capture its government through force, votes or moving people in.
taking-over-a-state-or-town.hook: Foreign governments, police and informers stop armed plots early. Towns remain under state and national law, so voters and courts there can only change what local government controls.
taking-over-a-state-or-town.can_you_build: The legal route is to move in and vote, as in Grafton, Marinaleda and New Hampshire. That wins local offices and leaves final authority where it was. Armed takeover is a crime in the places involved, and most confirmed attempts failed.

rules.cite: South African Civil Aviation Offences Act
rules.says: After the attempted coup in the Seychelles, South Africa charged the mercenaries over the hijacking of an Air India aircraft and not over the coup attempt.
The Oregon attorney general argued that Rajneeshpuram's creation as a city merged church and city. Federal and state courts later reached different results.

South African law made every Black South African a citizen of one of the homelands, territories set aside for them under apartheid. The Act said they stayed citizens of South Africa for purposes of international law.

facts: Comoros: the mercenary Bob Denard came with 43 men in 1978 and led a 500-strong guard for 11 years.
Seychelles: 53 mercenaries, with $300,000 raised against the $5 million advised.
Rajneeshpuram, Oregon: about 7,000 people on a ranch costing $5.75 million.
Free State Project, a plan for libertarians to move to New Hampshire: 20,000 pledges by 2016 and about 6,232 people moved by May 2022.

indigenous-prior-sovereignty.name: Indigenous peoples and authority older than the state
indigenous-prior-sovereignty.who_owns: Disputed. The peoples concerned assert authority that is older than the country, while the country usually treats the matter as domestic.
indigenous-prior-sovereignty.hook: Countries decide whether to accept the passports, recognise the government or pass the law. Courts rule on what the country's own laws mean, and a later case can narrow an earlier win.
indigenous-prior-sovereignty.can_you_build: This route is open only to a people with an existing claim. The known results came from negotiated land claims, court rulings and long use of a document, and each result stays within the existing country.

rules.says: Land reserved for the Muscogee Nation in the 19th century was never legally dissolved and remains 'Indian country', meaning land under tribal and federal authority, for the purposes of the Major Crimes Act, a federal law on serious crimes.
The federal government and the state of Oklahoma share the power to prosecute crimes committed by non-Native people against Native victims in Indian country.

rules.cite: Nunavut Act and Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act, 1993
rules.says: Created a territory for Inuit self-government within Canada.

facts: Nunavut: 2,093,190 km², 36,858 people in 2021, with the agreement approved by nearly 85% of voters.
The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy) have issued their own passport since at least 1923.
Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi, a Native Hawaiian self-government group, reported 21,000 members in 1997.

exile-and-landless-authority.who_owns: Someone else holds the land. The exile body holds a claim, a community and whatever standing others give it.
exile-and-landless-authority.hook: The country in control simply keeps the territory. The host country decides how much activity it allows, and other governments decide whether to deal with the exile body.
exile-and-landless-authority.can_you_build: Keep a body running abroad with elections, members and funding from people who left the homeland. The Tibetan and Belarusian cases show this can last for decades without gaining any territory.

rules.cite: Charter of the Tibetans in Exile, 1991, amended 2011
rules.says: Sets out the exile government's structure, with executive power held by an elected leader called the Sikyong.

rules.cite: Constitutive and declarative theories of recognition
rules.says: One view says a state exists only when others recognise it. The other says recognition is not required if the tests in the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty defining a state, are met.

facts: The Rada BNR, the council of the Belarusian Democratic Republic, has been in exile since 1919 and is described as the oldest existing government in exile as of 2026.
The Tibetan administration was re-established on 29 April 1959, and no country recognises it as sovereign.
The Sahrawi refugee camps, home to people from Western Sahara, hold 173,600 people, by a 2023 estimate.

digital-no-territory.who_owns: Each participant stays under the law of wherever they live, and each server sits under the law of where it is. A state needs a defined territory, so a project with none fails one of the four tests in the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty whose definition of a state is the usual checklist. It may still function as an association, a company or a club.
digital-no-territory.hook: Normal national law on tax, securities (investments sold to the public), payments and identity documents. Selling 'citizenships' or digital tokens brings securities and fraud law, plus the rules on money transfers set by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international body that writes anti-money-laundering standards.
digital-no-territory.can_you_build: Anyone can found one, at the cost of a website and a legal structure. It can run as a company registered in a real country. Estonia's model runs the other way: a real country keeps backup government data in a data centre in Luxembourg by agreement with that country.

rules.says: A defined territory is required.
Statehood does not depend on recognition, but reading this with Article 1 appears to keep the territory test in place.
A country-code web domain follows the ISO 3166 list, the international list of country codes. IANA, the body that manages these domains, says it does not decide what is a country.

Passport issuer codes come from the ISO 3166 agency or from separately listed organizations, under the passport standard of the International Civil Aviation Organization, the UN agency for civil flying.

facts: Asgardia, a self-declared space nation, reported more than 290,000 citizens in March 2019, according to Wikipedia, with no recognized territory.

Estonia's 'data embassy' is a Tier 4 (highest-reliability grade) data centre in Luxembourg, under an agreement between the two countries that takes account of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, the treaty on the rights of embassies.

no-territory-conceptual.who_owns: Nothing is owned, because nothing is claimed on the ground or the claim is carried with the person or object. The people involved remain under the law of the place where they stand.
no-territory-conceptual.hook: Your home country's law continues to apply. John Lennon and Yoko Ono, who declared the conceptual country of Nutopia, asked for diplomatic immunity, the legal protection given to diplomats. The published account records no grant of it. His deportation order was overturned in 1975, and he received a green card in 1976.
no-territory-conceptual.can_you_build: Anyone can declare one, and several have lasted decades as organizations. The published accounts report no recognition by any country.

rules.says: The founder of Slowjamastan, a self-declared micronation, cites the criteria in this 1933 treaty defining a state as the basis of its legitimacy. The published account does not list them, and it reports no legal recognition.

facts: Nutopia's anthem is four seconds of silence.
The territory of Obsidia is two portable pieces of obsidian, a volcanic glass.
Atlantium had almost 3,000 citizens as of 2015, most of whom signed up online.

statehood-criteria.need: Meet the four tests of statehood
statehood-criteria.what: The usual checklist comes from Article 1 of the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty that defines what a state is. It asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to deal with other countries. Article 3 says a state exists whether or not others recognize it. In practice, a platform with rotating staff struggles on population, a site with no territory fails the second test, and the capacity to deal with others depends on other countries being willing to talk. In 2010 the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, advised that general international law contains no applicable ban on declaring independence. That leaves open whether a declaration achieves anything.

territory-law.need: Have land the law lets you hold
territory-law.what: Almost every place outside a country is closed to claims by treaty. Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, artificial islands get no territorial sea, the belt of coastal water that land has (Article 60(8)), the high seas cannot be claimed (Article 89), and the deep seabed cannot be taken as anyone's own (Article 137). The Antarctic Treaty, which governs the continent, takes no new claims (Article IV). The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, bars any country from taking over space (Article II). The old route, occupying land that belongs to no one, is a method used by countries. In its Western Sahara opinion, the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, said the practice of countries at the relevant time did not treat land inhabited by socially and politically organized peoples as qualifying. That leaves two strips of land, Bir Tawil and Gornja Siga, each between neighbors with border guards.

un-admission.what: Article 4 of the UN Charter, the UN's founding treaty, opens membership to peace-loving states, by a decision of the General Assembly on a recommendation from the Security Council. The Council needs nine of its 15 votes, with no veto from any of the five permanent members (China, France, Russia, the UK and the US). The Assembly then needs a two-thirds majority of those present and voting. That means 129 yes votes out of 193, if all vote. South Sudan was the last to join, in 2011. Palestine and the Holy See, the government of the Catholic Church, sit as non-member observers.
un-admission.figure: 193 members; 9 of 15 votes in the Security Council with no vetoes; two-thirds in the General Assembly (129 if all 193 vote)

micro-precedents.need: Know how small a real country can be
micro-precedents.what: Size is no bar. Small countries counted by the World Bank in 2024 include Tuvalu with 9,646 people, Nauru with 11,947 and Palau with 17,695. All three hold natural land and are recognized by others. A new project's obstacle therefore lies in territory and consent, since a population of about 10,000 is already enough for a UN seat in practice. San Marino, Monaco and Liechtenstein have 34,000 to 40,000 people.

legal-personality.what: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, the treaty on how treaties work, applies to agreements between countries, and its Article 6 says every country can make them. To other countries, a 'treaty' signed by an unrecognized place would appear to be a private document. That matters because nearly every other requirement here runs on treaties: extradition, air services, post, tax and membership of the International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for radio coordination. The 2010 opinion on Kosovo by the International Court of Justice, the UN's top court, concerns only whether a declaration broke the law.
legal-personality.figure: Article 6: every state has the capacity to make treaties

iso-3166.what: ISO 3166 is the international list of two- and three-letter country codes, used by banks, shipping, airlines, web domains and passports. As reported on Wikipedia from the standard's Maintenance Agency, the office that keeps the list, the only way in is to be registered in either the UN Terminology Bulletin Country Names or the UN Statistics Division's Standard Country or Area Codes. Entry therefore depends on the UN. Kosovo uses XK, a code from the 'user-assigned' range, which sits outside the official list. This account rests on a secondary source, and the International Organization for Standardization's (ISO) own page was not reviewed.

cctld.what: Country web domains such as .fr are tied to the ISO 3166 list of country codes. RFC 1591, the 1994 document that set the policy, says the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA), which manages these domains, 'is not in the business of deciding what is and what is not a country', and that the ISO list was picked because ISO, the International Organization for Standardization, has a procedure for that decision. A new '.xx' domain therefore follows only after a place gets its ISO code. Anyone can still buy an ordinary .com or a domain under another country's code, which means your web address sits under another registry's rules.

ip-addresses.what: Blocks of IP addresses, the numbers that identify devices online, come from regional registries. ARIN, the North American registry, says businesses, nonprofits or government entities are eligible, including individuals who meet the legal requirements of the country where they do business. The normal route is therefore a registered legal entity in a real country. A self-declared state could only apply through a company elsewhere, or rely on an upstream provider, a company that supplies its internet connection. Either way, the provider's home country can cut service.

iso-4217.what: ISO 4217 is the international list of currency codes such as USD and EUR. SIX, the Swiss exchange group, is its official Maintenance Agency, the office that keeps the list, and calls itself the only recognized, authoritative source on currency codes. Codes matter because banks and trading systems use them to book payments. Without one, a currency would have no standard listing on normal payment systems, which appears to limit it to local paper money or a private token. The International Organization for Standardization's (ISO) own description of who may apply was not reviewed.

own-currency.need: Choose: own money, someone else's, or crypto
own-currency.what: Printing notes costs little, and Minerva, Sealand and New Utopia all produced a currency or pictures of one. Legal tender status means courts in your place accept the money to settle debts, which helps only where you have courts others respect. Outsiders will take your money only if they can swap it for something. Crypto looks like a way around this, yet the businesses that convert crypto to dollars are regulated in their home countries. Your people therefore end up subject to those countries' rules at the point of exchange.

fatf-travel-rule.what: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF), an international body, writes the standard that most countries' anti-money-laundering rules follow. Its Recommendation 16, the Travel Rule, requires financial institutions and virtual asset service providers (crypto businesses) to share who sent and who receives a transfer. For cross-border transfers above USD/EUR 1,000, the 2025 revision requires the name, account number and country and town of the person receiving the money. The revisions take effect at the end of 2030 and reach crypto firms indirectly, through FATF's Recommendation 15 on new technologies. This account comes from a law firm's summary and from Elliptic, a crypto analysis firm, and not from FATF's own text.

mica.what: The EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) sets uniform rules for crypto-assets not already covered by financial law, including asset-referenced and e-money tokens, which are types of stablecoin (crypto tokens tied to the value of something else, such as a currency). It requires white papers, the disclosure documents for a token, and official approval for service providers. Firms already operating before 30 December 2024 could continue only until 1 July 2026 or until a decision on their licence. Any citizen token sold to people in the EU now falls under these rules. A project may not be based in the EU, but its customers and exchanges are.
mica.figure: 1 July 2026: last date for the transition

genius.what: Stablecoins are crypto tokens tied to the value of a currency. The US GENIUS Act of 2025 (Public Law 119-27) says US issuers of these tokens need approval from a state or federal regulator and must hold at least one dollar of permitted reserves for each dollar issued. Issuers above $50 billion must file audited statements. Exchanges in the US may offer foreign stablecoins only under set conditions, and the Treasury may arrange 'reciprocal' deals with places that have comparable rules. An unrecognized place appears to have no regulator for the Treasury to deal with. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), a US bank regulator, has issued final rules, and the Treasury proposed more in 2026.
genius.figure: $1 reserve per $1 issued; audited statements above $50 billion

correspondent-banking.need: Get a bank to handle your payments
correspondent-banking.what: International payments travel between banks that hold accounts with each other, called correspondent banks. A new place with no banking law or supervisor gives them no one to rely on. The Financial Stability Board, an international body that monitors the financial system, reports a steady fall in those relationships. Active correspondents dropped 3.9% in 2016, 4.1% in 2017 and 3.4% in 2018, with US dollar links falling fastest and smaller, higher-risk places hit hardest. This retreat is called de-risking. Without a correspondent, your people cannot receive a wire transfer. Newer data has not been reviewed.

swift.need: Get access to SWIFT, the bank messaging network
swift.what: SWIFT is the messaging network banks use to instruct payments. Regional law binds it: in March 2022, an EU regulation banned the service for seven Russian banks. SWIFT's own eligibility criteria are not quoted here. The practical path for a new place is a licensed bank, which needs a licensing authority other countries accept. Crypto payment systems avoid SWIFT, and they then run into the exchange and stablecoin rules described in the other entries.

fatf-grey.need: Stay off the grey list for weak money-laundering rules
fatf-grey.what: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international body that sets anti-money-laundering standards, lists places with weak rules. A paper at the International Monetary Fund by Kida and Paetzold estimates that being on this 'grey list' cuts capital inflows by about 7.6% of GDP, the yearly value of a country's economy. After the June 2026 meeting, 22 places were on the list, and an industry summary reports four removals in October 2026 (Bulgaria, Monaco, Côte d'Ivoire and DR Congo), which would leave 18 if none were added. Iran, North Korea and Myanmar are on a separate high-risk list. A place FATF has never assessed would appear to have no clean record to show banks.

passports-icao.need: Issue a passport other countries accept
passports-icao.what: Doc 9303, a standard from the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency for civil flying, sets the passport format. Part 3 says the codes for issuing countries come from the agency that keeps the ISO 3166 country code list, plus separate lists for bodies such as the UN and INTERPOL. Recognized passports therefore link back to the UN lists that feed ISO 3166. ICAO has 193 member countries. Joining under the Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, means being a UN member, or winning four-fifths of ICAO's Assembly with UN approval (Articles 92 and 93). Printing a booklet in this format still gets no code on these lists, so machine readers and border systems would appear to have no entry for it.
passports-icao.figure: 193 ICAO members; 4/5 vote for countries outside the UN

camouflage-passports.need: Stay clear of fantasy and camouflage passports
camouflage-passports.what: A camouflage passport looks real but names a country or body that does not exist. A fantasy passport is a similar novelty, not valid for travel. Sealand's passports were called fantasy passports by the Council of the EU, according to Wikipedia. The EU glossary itself has not been reviewed. In 1997, the Bates family, who run Sealand, revoked them after finding an international money-laundering ring using them. In US law it is a crime to falsely make 'any passport or instrument purporting to be a passport' intended for use, and to use one (18 USC 1543). Using one at a border may bring charges under such laws.

citizenship-tax-us.need: Know that new citizenship leaves US tax in place
citizenship-tax-us.what: The US taxes its citizens on worldwide income wherever they live. The Supreme Court upheld this in Cook v. Tait (1924), for a citizen living in Mexico with Mexican income. The duty follows citizenship, so joining a micronation (a self-declared small country) appears to change nothing. Americans abroad must still file. Anyone hoping to live on a platform tax-free therefore faces a tax return every year until they formally give up US nationality. Giving it up without holding another nationality leaves a person stateless. The State Department warns that a stateless person lacks the protection of any government and may have difficulty traveling.

renunciation.need: Renounce US citizenship and pay the exit bill
renunciation.what: Giving up US citizenship formally costs a government fee. The fee was $2,350 from 2015 until a final rule published in March 2026 cut it to $450, so the $2,350 figure often quoted is out of date. Separately, 'covered expatriates' pay an exit tax. That means anyone with $2 million or more in net worth, or average income tax above $211,000 a year (2026 figure), or who has not certified five years of tax compliance. They are treated as selling all their assets the day before leaving, after an exclusion of $910,000 for 2026.
renunciation.figure: $450 fee since March 2026 (was $2,350); $2 million net-worth test

fatca-crs.what: Foreign banks report US account holders to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), the US tax agency, under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA). Americans must also report foreign financial assets above set limits. Many other countries swap account data under the Common Reporting Standard of the OECD, a club of mostly wealthy countries. A report on the Global Forum, the international group that oversees this exchange, gives 171 million accounts worth nearly EUR 13 trillion, 172 member countries and territories, and about EUR 135 billion in extra revenue. Your bank therefore tells your home tax office you have the account, whichever flag you live under. These figures come from a news summary, and the OECD's report page did not show them.

ship-flag.need: Fly a real country's flag or risk being boarded
ship-flag.what: On the high seas, meaning open ocean outside any country's control, a ship needs a country's flag, with a 'genuine link' to that country (Article 91 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, or UNCLOS, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans). Warships may board on suspicion of no nationality (Article 110(1)(d)). A ship using several flags may be treated as having none (Article 92(2)). In US drug law, a 'vessel without nationality' includes one whose claimed registry is denied by the nation named, or whose captain makes no claim when asked (46 USC 70502). A real flag means living under that country's law and its duties on safety and crew (Article 94). Choosing the flag of a country with no coast is allowed (Article 90), since any country may run a register.

boarding-offences.need: Avoid the acts that let foreign warships board you
boarding-offences.what: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, three acts open a ship to foreign warships regardless of flag, in the broadcasting case only if the warship's country has legal power under Article 109. Piracy: any country may seize a pirate ship and try those aboard (Article 105), and piracy covers violence or detention for private ends against another ship or in a place outside any country's control (Article 101). Slave trade: suspicion allows a warship to stop and inspect (Article 110), and a slave who reaches any ship is free (Article 99). Unauthorized broadcasting: any country receiving the signal or suffering interference may arrest the person and seize the equipment (Article 109). Funding a project through a pirate radio station therefore invites arrest.
boarding-offences.figure: 5 kinds of country can prosecute unauthorized broadcasts

crime.need: Decide who prosecutes crime on your platform
crime.what: With no recognized court, the answer is any country with a link to the case. The country whose flag or register covers the structure applies its law. A person's own country often does too: US law reaches 'any place outside the jurisdiction of any nation' for offenses by or against a US national (18 USC 7(7)). Other countries may act on piracy or broadcasting. Your own court's verdict would not be accepted by others as binding, and locking someone up on your platform appears able to count as kidnapping or unlawful detention under the law of their home country.

extradition.what: Extradition, the handing over of a person to another country to face charges, runs on treaties between governments. In US law, a judge's power starts with 'a treaty or convention for extradition' with a foreign government (18 USC 3184). A place with no treaties cannot ask for anyone back. Countries where your citizens travel can still hand them over to third countries under their own treaties. A fugitive from one country therefore gains little from a flag, and your residents can be arrested as soon as they land in a port. In Thailand's 2019 case, the navy raided a floating home and filed a police complaint over an offense it said carries life imprisonment or death.

force-record.need: Defend it, or know the record
force-record.what: Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, the UN's founding treaty, bars force in its members' international relations against 'any state', which appears to offer an unrecognized project little protection. Italy took Rose Island 56 days after its declaration and bombed it. Tonga claimed the Minerva Reefs within weeks and removed later occupiers with troops. Thailand raided a seastead, a floating home at sea, in 2019 and raised the death penalty. Croatia has jailed and fined visitors to Liberland. Sealand survived an armed takeover by hired mercenaries in 1978, and Britain later placed it within its waters by law. In Antarctica and on the Moon, military bases are barred by treaty for the countries that have joined.

rescue.need: Plan for medical care and rescue
rescue.what: Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the treaty that sets the rules for the oceans, ship captains must rescue people in danger at sea (Article 98), so a nearby ship should come, and coastal countries run search-and-rescue services for their waters. After rescue you land in someone else's country, under its law. If spacecraft crew land in distress on a member country's territory or on the high seas, members must help them and return them to the launching authority (Rescue Agreement, a treaty on helping astronauts, Articles 2 to 4; Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, Article V). That authority is a country or a qualifying international organization, so a self-declared state appears to have no standing. A hospital of your own is a cost in the budget, and specialist care means going ashore.

sanctions.what: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the US sanctions office, binds all US citizens and permanent residents wherever they are located, plus US entities and their foreign branches. The property of blocked people must be frozen. EU sanctions cut seven Russian banks from SWIFT, the bank messaging network, in 2022, and the rule extended to entities they own by 50% or more. Any US person who helps a listed person at your project therefore appears to take on personal legal exposure, wherever the project sits. OFAC publishes tables of civil penalties each year.

securities-fraud.need: Avoid securities fraud when selling land or bonds
securities-fraud.what: Selling a stake in a future country to the public can count as selling securities, the investments regulated by financial law. In 1999 the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the regulator of investment markets, sued Lazarus Long, born Howard Turney, over a $350 million bond offering at 9.5% interest for 'New Utopia', a Caribbean nation that had not been built. The court froze the funds, and in January 2000 he consented to a permanent injunction, a court order banning the conduct. He had raised $24,000, and the order to hand the money back was waived because he could not pay. The charges were under Securities Act Sections 5 and 17(a) and Exchange Act Section 10(b). Citizenship tokens with a promised return carry the same risk.

lunar-deeds.need: Understand what a lunar deed is worth
lunar-deeds.what: Dennis Hope's Lunar Embassy has sold acres of the Moon since 1980. Discover magazine reported 4.25 million buyers and over $9 million in sales at $19.99, and National Geographic reported 2.5 million plots at $22.49. The Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, bars any country from taking over the Moon, and the Moon Agreement, a separate treaty with few members, bars private property in the surface for its members. The International Institute of Space Law, a professional body of space lawyers, issued a statement warning that such deeds could mislead individuals. No court or government registry backing them has been found. Buyers receive a printed deed.

launch-licence.what: A US launch needs a licence from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the US aviation regulator, as does any launch by a US citizen outside the US (51 USC 50904). The licence rules are in 14 CFR Part 450. The licence holder must carry insurance for harm to others, sized to the 'maximum probable loss' and capped at $500 million or the most available on the world market at a reasonable cost (51 USC 50914; 14 CFR 440.9). The payload must also comply with US law, and the government can block a launch on safety, national security or foreign policy grounds. A US launch therefore brings US supervision with it.

space-registration.need: Register your spacecraft with a country
space-registration.what: The Registration Convention, the treaty on listing objects launched into space, requires a launching country to register each object and give the UN its orbit and purpose (Articles II and IV). The registering country then keeps legal power and control over the object and anyone aboard (Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, Article VIII). This is the central obstacle for any orbital nation. Only launching countries, and international organizations that accept the Convention, run these registers (Articles II and VII), and being on a country's register puts you under that country. The Convention has 77 members. It appears to give private people no way to register themselves.

liability-convention.need: Pay for damage from your spacecraft
liability-convention.what: Under the Liability Convention, the treaty on who pays for damage from space objects, a launching country must pay for damage its object causes on Earth or to aircraft, with no need to prove fault (Article II). In space, it pays only if at fault (Article III). Countries that launch together share the liability (Article V). A launching country includes one that launches, pays for the launch, or whose territory is used (Article I). The Convention has 100 members. A country exposed in this way appears to have good reason to require licensing and insurance before a launch.

spectrum.need: Get radio frequencies through a member country
spectrum.what: Spacecraft and many ships need radio frequencies, which are coordinated by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency for radio coordination. Its founding treaty, the ITU Constitution, treats frequencies and orbits as limited natural resources (Article 44) and bars harmful interference (Article 45). National authorities submit notices of frequency assignments, which are entered in the Master International Frequency Register, the official global list. The ITU has 194 member countries. Countries outside the UN can apply only with the agreement of two-thirds of members under Article 2(c). A self-declared state therefore needs a member to file for it, which puts that member's regulator in charge.

air-routes.need: Win flight rights and landing rights
air-routes.what: Under the Chicago Convention, the treaty that sets the rules for international civil flying, scheduled international air service needs special permission from each country flown over or landed in (Article 6). Non-scheduled flights have more freedom, but only for aircraft of countries that have joined the treaty (Article 5). Every aircraft has one country of registration and must carry its marks (Articles 17 to 20). An airline from an unrecognized place therefore cannot use these rights, since it has no member country behind it. The workaround is to rely on aircraft registered in another country. Pilotless craft need separate permission (Article 8).

environment.what: Each place has its own process. Article 28 of the BBNJ Agreement, the treaty on marine life in waters outside any country's control, has required its members to assess the impact of planned activities in those areas since January 2026. Antarctica requires an assessment beforehand under Article 8 of the Madrid Protocol, an add-on to the Antarctic Treaty, and Article 7 bans mining. At sea, the London Protocol, a treaty on dumping, treats dumping as forbidden unless permitted. Members of the Outer Space Treaty, the main treaty on space, must avoid harmful contamination (Article IX), and COSPAR, an international space science committee, sets standards on protecting other planets. The South China Sea tribunal, a panel of judges under the law-of-the-sea treaty, held that building land at seven reefs breached a country's duties on the marine environment. If your home country has joined these treaties, it may apply these rules to you through its own law.

food-water-power.what: No project in the published sources has produced its own food at scale. A person needs about 0.84 kg of oxygen a day, according to NASA, and food use on the International Space Station (ISS) ran at 2.77 kg per crew member per day. The ISS has reached 98% water recovery, and it still relies on deliveries for tanks, water bags and food. At sea, a platform needs a port. Oceanix's Busan design, a planned floating district in South Korea, intends to make its own energy on site, though that remains a plan. Dependence on a neighbor's port appears to give that neighbor leverage. Italy blockaded Rose Island after seizing it, to stop anyone from returning.
food-water-power.figure: 0.84 kg oxygen and 2.77 kg food per person per day

population.what: The Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty that defines what a state is, asks for a permanent population without giving a number. Tuvalu has 9,646 people. A model by the researcher Salotti in the journal Scientific Reports puts the minimum for a self-sustaining Mars colony at 110, based on labor time and under strong assumptions. The rule of thumb from these cases is that a society can be small on paper, while a working one needs doctors, engineers, teachers and courts. Sealand shows the limit: Wikipedia reports one permanent resident as of August 2024, and the Minnesota Journal of Law, Science and Technology reported two in 2019.

cost-floating.what: Published figures are all estimates for things not yet built. Oceanix Busan, in South Korea: $200 million stated in 2021, or $627 million at the developers' $10,000 per square metre, for 15.5 acres and 12,000 people. Freedom Ship: as high as about $16 billion for 80,000 people, stalled for decades. Pangeos: about $8 billion for 60,000. A law journal puts even a small deep-sea platform for a few residents at $50 million. By simple arithmetic on those numbers, the cost per resident runs from about $17,000 to $200,000 for the larger plans, and far more for a small platform.

cost-orbit.what: Jones, writing for NASA, calculated $54,500 per kg for the Space Shuttle to low orbit, and $2,720 per kg for SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket at its 2018 price of $62 million. By early 2026, a full Falcon 9 for one customer was about $74 million, or $3,246 per kg at full capacity. A shared flight starts at $350,000 for 50 kg. Voyager's filings imply $90 million for a Starship flight, once certified, according to Motley Fool's reading of them. Those are rocket costs alone. Food, at 2.77 kg a day, comes to about 1,000 kg a person each year, or about $3.3 million at the Falcon 9 rate, by simple arithmetic.

cost-station.what: The International Space Station (ISS) costs about $3 billion a year to run, according to NASA's Inspector General. Vast, a private space station company, has committed more than $1 billion to its single-module Haven-1 station, which has slipped to no earlier than the first quarter of 2027, and it had sold no crew seat as of that report. Axiom, a private space company, gave a price of $55 million a seat for a 10-day trip to the ISS, plus NASA charges reported then as $2,000 per person per day for food and more for support.
cost-station.figure: $3 billion a year (ISS); $55 million per seat

buyers.what: The published record is mostly online sign-ups and small purchases. Lunar deed buyers number in the millions at about $20 each. Liberland reported hundreds of thousands of applications. Asgardia reported more than 290,000 citizens in 2019 and over 500,000 sign-ups within three weeks. New Utopia raised $24,000 against a $350 million offer. Próspera, a special zone in Honduras, drew foreign investors, and its claim against Honduras has fallen from $10.775 billion to $1.63 billion. Real second citizenship has a market too, as with the programme of St Kitts and Nevis, running since 1984.
